newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bank secrecy under fire in Holocaust debate.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank secrecy under fire in Holocaust debate.

text.p: Switzerland's bank secrecy laws, attacked by Jewish groups as a tool for hiding money lost in the Holocaust, faced pressure at home Sunday as politicians from government parties suggested the rules should be relaxed.

Swiss banks bowed four days ago to international protests and published an unprecedented list of dormant Holocaust-era accounts. On Sunday, leaders from two of four parties in the centre-right government coalition were quoted as saying it was time for more openness.
"A relaxation of bank secrecy seems to be possible now and the SP (Social Democratis Party) is interested in this," SP secretary general Barbara Haering-Binder told the newspaper Sonntags Zeitung.

"The existing rules do not make enough distinctions. We have to improve them quickly," Eugen David, member of parliament and economic policy expert for the Christian Democratic People's Party, told the paper.

David proposed rules on dormant accounts, such as those left from the Holocaust, that would require banks to search actively for customers who had not been heard from for a long time. Banks are not currently bound to seek the owners of dormant accounts.

The calls echoed recent proposals from an increasingly vocal group of members of parliament, mostly from the political left, for a legislative response to international furore over the banks' reluctance to open their Holocaust-era books.

But the idea that strict confidentiality laws, at the heart of Swiss banking since the 1930s, should be cut back also prompted quick rebuttals within the coalition, signalling what could be a long and difficult debate.
"This is nothing but wishful thinking and must not be allowed to happen," member of parliament Walther Frey, from the right-wing Swiss People's Party said.

The controversy started when a Jewish leader on Thursday predicted the end of Swiss bank secrecy was near after the banks, under international pressure, last week published over 1,870 names of owners of nearly 1,800 dormant accounts.

World Jewish Congress leader Edgar Bronfman Sr, who has led a two-year campaign to force open Swiss bank records on Holocaust-era accounts, said bank secrecy would end when another tranche of 20,000 or more pre-1945 accounts is published in October.
Swiss banks have kept account information strictly to themselves since laws passed in 1930s that barred them from handing over customer records to outsiders.

The new laws were attractive to German and other European Jews who were increasingly seeking a refuge for their money from the growing Nazi threat -- as well as to tax evaders from Switzerland's neighbouring countries.

The WJC says the same laws later helped banks hide an unknown amount of money left by Jews and others killed in the Holocaust, although the banks say they are not deliberately keeping assets back from the rightful heirs.
Since the early 1990s, the Swiss government has rolled back some key points of secrecy as part of international efforts to combat money-laundering by organised crime.

Bankers who under the old law where prohibited from reporting suspect transactions are now required to tell police about dubious cash movements. But the new rules only apply to suspected cases of money-laundering.
